headline: Race Ebb at 3.8 Knots: Bass Go Nocturnal, Sea Bass Rule Plum Gut by Day
subhead: The Sound's thermal split is rewriting the clock on the bass bite while Plum Gut's hard bottom keeps quietly loading the cooler.
body_markdown:
3.8 knots on the tail end of Tuesday's ebb through The Race — that's down from the 5-plus we were riding around the new moon two weeks back, and it tells you almost everything you need to know about this week. We're sliding toward the first quarter on the 21st, current's easing off the peak, and that softer push is exactly why the bite windows have stretched out instead of snapping shut in twenty minutes like they do on the big tides.

Here's the other number that matters: Kings Point is reading 71.6, New London's sitting at 67.6. That's a four-degree spread across maybe fifteen miles of open Sound, and it's steep enough to change how these fish behave, not just where they hold. Striped bass hate that upper-60s-to-low-70s window during daylight — it's not that they've left, it's thermal avoidance, pure and simple. They're dropping into the deeper structure around Race Rock and Valiant Rock during the day and doing their real feeding after dark when the surface layer cools a notch and the bait comes up off bottom.

So that's where I've been putting my trips. Valiant Rock's slack window this week is running about 20 to 25 minutes after New London's posted high — close enough to the book that you can plan around it, but I'm still checking it against the actual boil before I commit gear. Wire line with a big tube-and-worm or a bunker spoon, worked through 25 to 40 feet on the drop from max current into that slack, has been the move for the bigger fish. If you're bucktail guys, go heavy — 3 to 4 ounces with a white or chartreuse curly tail — and fish it on the last hour of the ebb before the rock stops boiling, then again as the flood builds back. Night trips through Race Rock and down into the Sluiceway have put mid-30s and a few upper-30s in the box on eels drifted naturally with the current, no weight, just letting the tide do the work.

During daylight, forget the bass and go to Plum Gut, because that's where the sure thing is right now. Black sea bass have been outstanding on the hard bottom there — 35 to 55 feet, bucktail-and-Gulp combos or just a plain jig-and-bait rig with squid strips, dropped tight to the rocks on the up-current side. We had a 28-inch fish come out of there this past week, which tells you the resident population on that structure is mature and it's holding. Fluke are riding shotgun on the same drifts — keeper-class fish, nothing huge, but steady, on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and bucktails in the 3/4 to 1-ounce range depending on how hard the Gut is running that particular stage. The Gut doesn't care what the surface temp is doing up top; that current keeps it well-oxygenated and the bait pinned, so it's been the most dependable piece of water in the whole zone this month.

Little Gull and Great Gull have been quieter than I'd like for daytime bass, which tracks with the thermal read — that shallower structure warms fast and the fish are ghosting off it until the sun goes down. If you want a shot at bass in daylight, work the deeper current seams off the northeast side of Great Gull on the last of the ebb, right where the rip line goes glassy for a few boat-lengths. That seam has produced a handful of upper-slot fish on wire and umbrella rigs, but it's not a sure thing — I'd call it two good trips out of five this past stretch, and you need the tide stage dialed in tight.

No bluefish push into the eastern Sound yet, though the blitz pattern working the bunker schools from the Jersey shore up through western Long Island is the kind of thing that spreads if the calm weather holds — worth watching the Race and Fishers Island Sound over the next week or two for blues to show up chasing the same bunker north. And no albies or bonito in the Gut yet either — that's a straight watch item. Squid are building around Rhode Island and into Nantucket Sound as that water pushes into the high 50s and low 60s inshore, which is the setup piece that usually precedes the first scout fish showing at Montauk or the Vineyard. If that squid keeps building, I'd expect the first false albacore sniffs in our waters sometime in the first half of August, not before.

Looking ahead: as we ease into that first quarter moon, currents through The Race and Plum Gut will keep softening through the weekend, which favors slower presentations — slow-trolled tube-and-worm over fast-stripped bucktails, patient drifts over Plum Gut instead of covering water. If the stable weather holds, I'd fish the night tide at Race Rock for bass and hit Plum Gut in daylight for a mixed bag of sea bass and fluke — that's the two-part game plan that's actually been producing, not the exciting story, but the honest one.
